title: Who took part
text: The IP-PAD UK data bring together four online surveys with 4,968 interviews in total. Two were carried out by Gallup International and two by Survation, and each provider ran two waves about a year apart. Because the surveys reached different age groups in different ways, it helps to know who took part before reading any comparison between them, and this page serves as the background for the other insights.

title: Who took part
section: Two ways of reaching young people
text:
Two ways of reaching young people
Gallup International interviewed members of its online access panels aged 16 and over, who answered every question themselves. Survation, in turn, reached children through parents on its online panels. A parent gave consent and reported the child’s age, gender, region and type of place, and then handed the device to the child, who answered all remaining questions. In the Survation surveys, the background information thus comes from parents, while the questions on politics and on household income were answered by the young people themselves.

title: Who took part
text:
Age

Each panel shows one survey. The bars give the number of respondents at each year of age, on a shared age axis from 12 to 26.










The two providers cover different stages of youth. Survation W1 includes ages 12 to 17 and Survation W2 ages 12 to 18, with a median age of 15 in both. Gallup W1 covers ages 16 to 21, and Gallup W2 added a separate sample of young adults, so that it spans ages 16 to 26 with a median of 21. The providers thus overlap only at ages 16 to 18, and even there the numbers are uneven. Gallup has 167 respondents aged 16 or 17 in W1 and 121 in W2, and Survation W2 has only 25 respondents aged 18. Interestingly, Gallup W2 has 332 respondents aged 25, compared with at most 239 at any other age, a peak that the fieldwork documents do not explain.

title: Who took part
text:
When the surveys took place

Each row is one survey. The height of a bar shows the share of that survey’s interviews carried out in a given month. The dashed line marks the general election of 4 July 2024.










The wave number does not order the surveys in time. Gallup W1 was fielded in May and June 2024, during the campaign for the general election of July 2024 and thus still under a Conservative government. Survation W1 followed a year later, in the summer of 2025. Gallup W2 started in May 2025, but 95% of its interviews took place in November and December 2025, after Survation W1. Survation W2 then ran in the autumn of 2026. All surveys but the first therefore took place under a Labour government, and any difference between them can reflect the time of fieldwork as well as the age of the respondents.

title: Who took part
text:
Gender, place, education and income

Each row is one answer, grouped by question. The dots show the share of respondents in each survey who gave that answer.










In terms of gender and place, the four samples look much alike. Between 48% and 51% of respondents in each survey are female, and 24 respondents in total describe their gender in another way. Most live in a large town or city, from 44% in Survation W2 to 62% in Survation W1, and every UK region is represented. Education, however, mostly follows age, as it combines the level that respondents are studying for with the highest level attained by those who have left education. In the Survation surveys, 72% of respondents are in the lowest group (ISCED 0 to 2), which mainly reflects that most of them are still working towards their GCSEs. In Gallup, by contrast, 35% of those aged 18 to 21 and 66% of those aged 22 to 26 are studying for or hold a tertiary qualification (ISCED 5 to 8).
The question on household income shows a less expected pattern. In both Gallup surveys, 38% say that their household is living comfortably on its present income. In Survation W1 this share is 52%, but in Survation W2 it is only 30%, although both surveys used the same design. Young adolescents may find this question hard to judge, and the difference could also reflect who took part in each survey, so we would not read it as a change in household finances.

title: Who took part
text:
Fresh and recontacted respondents
In both second waves, the providers first invited their earlier respondents again, but few took part, namely 55 in Gallup W2 (5.6% of Gallup W1) and 72 in Survation W2 (7.3% of Survation W1). The rest of each sample was new. The data therefore come from 4,841 different young people, and each survey is best treated as a separate snapshot rather than as a panel.

title: Who took part
text:
About these data
The data are not weighted, so the shares on this page describe the respondents rather than all young people in the UK. Each provider also set its own quotas and its own rules for removing low quality interviews. The data page describes the design in detail.

title: The same young people a year later
text: Comparing young people of different ages says little about how the views of any one person develop. Both providers therefore re-interviewed some of their respondents. Gallup interviewed 55 young people in both waves, first in May 2024 and again in 2025, and Survation interviewed 72 young people in August 2025 and again in September 2026. This page asks how much their answers changed on average, and how stable they were from one person to the next.

title: The same young people a year later
text:
How certain the links are
Because the interviews were more than a year apart, a correctly linked respondent should be one or two years older in the second wave and report the same gender. The rule that Survation documented, which also accepts an unchanged age, is met by 52 of 55 Gallup links and 60 of 72 Survation links. A stricter rule, which requires an age one or two years higher, is met by only 48 and 39 links. Since Survation reached children through a parent’s panel account, some second interviews may have been answered by a sibling. We therefore show each result for all links and, as a check, for the strict links only.

title: The same young people a year later
text:
Average change is small

Each dot is the average change from the first to the second wave, with a line for its 95% confidence interval, and open circles repeat it for the strict links only. To compare measures, all are expressed in points of a scale from 0 to 10. Survation did not ask about trust or the progressive-conservative scale in its second wave.










On most measures, the average answers barely moved. The clearest change is that the Gallup panel felt less warmly about the Labour Party, by 1.1 points (95% interval of the change −1.8 to −0.4) on the scale from 0 to 10, and this holds for the strict links. As the general election of July 2024 fell between the two Gallup waves, this could reflect Labour’s move from opposition into government rather than anything specific to young people. In the Survation panel, feelings about Labour rose by 0.64 points (95% interval of the change 0.02 to 1.25), and certainty about one’s own beliefs fell by 4.4 points (95% interval of the change −8.5 to −0.3) on a scale from 0 to 100. However, neither Survation change is clear when only the strict links are kept.

title: The same young people a year later
section: Individual answers move more than the averages
text:
Individual answers move more than the averages

The bars show how many young people moved by a given number of points on the left-right scale. The shaded band marks a change of at most one point.










Behind these small averages, individuals move in both directions. On the left-right scale, 53% of the Gallup panel and 54% of the Survation panel chose the same point twice, but 18% of the Survation panel moved by three points or more. Those who started near the ends of the scale tended to move towards the centre. The 11 Survation respondents who first placed themselves at 3 or below moved right by 2.0 points on average, and the 12 who started at 7 or above moved left by 2.2. Measurement error alone would produce this pattern, since an answer that is extreme partly by chance tends to be less extreme the next time, so it does not necessarily mean that these young people became more moderate.

title: The same young people a year later
text:
How stable answers are

Each dot is the correlation between the answers in the two waves. A value of 1 means that everyone kept their position relative to the others, and 0 that the first answer says nothing about the second. Open circles show the strict links only.










Most correlations between the waves lie between 0.5 and 0.7, so young people largely keep their position relative to each other, even though single answers vary. Left-right self-placement is the most stable measure in Gallup, with a correlation of 0.80, but the least stable in Survation, with 0.42, or 0.48 with the strict links only. One possible reason is that many of the 12 to 17 year olds in Survation may not yet have a settled sense of what left and right mean.

title: The same young people a year later
text:
About these data
The two panels are small and include only those who agreed to take part again, who may differ from those who did not return. One difference is already visible. Survation W1 as a whole gives higher answers on the scales from 0 to 10 than the other surveys, with an average left-right position of 6.1, but its later panel members placed themselves at 5.1 in the first wave, close to the other surveys (4.4 to 5.0). The higher scores of Survation W1 thus come from those who did not return. In addition, the changes shown here combine real change with measurement error and possibly some wrongly linked respondents, and they cannot tell us why views changed. With 50 to 70 people per panel, only large changes can be detected with confidence. The data page explains the design of the surveys.

title: Views on the economy, morality, climate and immigration
text: Left and right are broad labels, and young people who share one can still disagree on concrete questions. All four surveys therefore asked how far respondents agree with fourteen statements on the economy, moral questions, climate change and immigration, with the option to say that they did not know. Some statements are worded so that agreeing expresses a left-leaning or progressive view, and others so that it expresses a right-leaning or conservative one. This mix helps to tell genuine views apart from a general tendency to agree.

title: Views on the economy, morality, climate and immigration
section: Broad agreement, with more division on welfare and immigration
text:
Broad agreement, with more division on welfare and immigration

Each bar shows the answers to one statement, with disagreement to the left and agreement to the right of the centre line. Neutral answers are split evenly across it, and the narrow column gives the share who did not know. All four surveys are pooled.










On moral questions and climate change, clear majorities take the progressive side. About two thirds agree that one parent can raise a child as well as two (67%) and that terminally ill people should have a right to assisted dying (69%), while the opposite statements on discrimination against women and on climate change find more disagreement than agreement. On the economy, however, the answers fit less neatly into one position. Most agree that the government should reduce income differences (68%), yet 51% also accept large income differences as a reward for talent and effort, and slightly more agree than disagree that welfare benefits make people lazy. These patterns hold within each survey.
Immigration divides young people most, and it is also the issue on which the surveys differ most. In Survation W2, 47% agree that immigration makes the UK a worse place to live, compared with 34% in Survation W1 about a year earlier, although both surveys cover the same ages. This could reflect a change over time, but it could equally reflect differences in who took part or in question order, as Survation W2 asked these statements after an experiment on ideology.

title: Views on the economy, morality, climate and immigration
section: Gender gaps are largest on questions about gender and family
text:
Gender gaps are largest on questions about gender and family

Each row compares the share of young women and young men who agree with a statement in one survey. A longer line means a larger gap.










Young women and young men differ most on statements about gender and the family. Young women more often agree that one parent can raise a child as well as two, with gaps of between 6 and 16 percentage points, and less often that discrimination against women is no longer a problem. These gaps are larger among the Gallup respondents than among the 12 to 17 year olds in Survation, whose gender was reported by a parent. On climate change, a gap appears in Gallup only, where young men more often see its impact as exaggerated.

title: Views on the economy, morality, climate and immigration
section: Older respondents agree more, on both sides
text:
Older respondents agree more, on both sides

Each panel shows one statement in Gallup W2, with the share who agree in each age group and a line for the 95% confidence interval. The lower row holds the counterparts of the statements in the upper row.










Since each survey covers different ages, we look at age within Gallup W2, the only survey that spans ages 16 to 26. Interestingly, older respondents there agree more often with statements on both sides of the same issue. Agreement that the government should reduce income differences rises from 62% among 16 and 17 year olds to 71% among 22 to 26 year olds, but agreement that large income differences are acceptable rises as well, from 37% to 54%. This suggests that older respondents are, if anything, more willing to agree in general rather than more left or more right. Differences in who took part at each age could also play a role, and only 121 respondents are aged 16 or 17.

title: Views on the economy, morality, climate and immigration
text:
Few answer “I don’t know”

Each dot is the share of “I don’t know” answers across all fourteen statements, at one year of age in one survey. Ages with fewer than 20 respondents are left out.










Only 3% of all answers are “I don’t know”. In the two Survation surveys, 12 to 14 year olds choose it somewhat more often (5% of their answers) than 15 to 17 year olds (3%), most of all for the statement on assisted dying. Gallup W2 has the fewest such answers at every age, so the differences between surveys are as large as those between ages.

title: Views on the economy, morality, climate and immigration
text:
About these data
The overview pools all interviews, so Gallup W2, which is twice as large as the other surveys, counts twice as much. The surveys are unweighted and differ in age range, recruitment and timing (see The data), which is why we compare age and gender within surveys. Gallup W1 also shows signs of weaker response quality. The statements that immigration enriches cultural life and that it makes the UK a worse place should go together negatively, as they do in the other surveys with correlations between −0.37 and −0.33. In Gallup W1, however, the correlation is only −0.03. Leaving Gallup W1 out changes no pooled share of agreement by more than 2 percentage points.

title: Explore
Explore
About
text:
IP-PAD, short for Interdisciplinary Perspectives on the Politics of Adolescence and Democracy, is a Doctoral Network funded by the European Union under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) of Horizon Europe. The network starts from the idea that adolescence and early adulthood, roughly the years between 11 and 21, are a formative period for political attitudes. During these years, young people’s cognitive abilities, emotions and social lives change considerably. We ask how these changes shape the way young people process political information, and in turn how they come to engage with politics.
Because no single discipline can answer this question on its own, IP-PAD brings together political science, political and social psychology, developmental neuroscience and affective science. At the same time, the network trains a cohort of doctoral candidates who carry out their research across these fields.
One part of this work is a panel survey of young people in five countries, Austria, Greece, the Netherlands, Poland and the United Kingdom. The surveys share a common set of questions and invite respondents back in later waves, so that political and psychological development can be followed over time and compared between countries. This website presents the data from the United Kingdom, where the surveys are led by the team at Royal Holloway, University of London. The data page describes how the UK surveys were carried out.

title: The data
text: The IP-PAD UK data come from four online surveys of young people in the United Kingdom, carried out between 2024 and 2026. Two fieldwork providers each ran two waves. Gallup International interviewed young people who are members of its online panels themselves, while Survation reached younger adolescents through the panel accounts of their parents. We combined the four surveys into one data file with one row per interview, which holds 4,968 interviews with 4,841 young people. Apart from two questions about the future that only Survation asked, the file includes only questions that were asked in at least two of the surveys, so that answers can be compared between them.

title: The data
section: When the surveys were in the field
text:
When the surveys were in the field

Each row shows one survey. The bars give the number of interviews in each month, on the same scale for all four surveys.










Three of the surveys carried out most of their interviews within two or three months. Gallup W2 is the exception. It began in May 2025 with a small number of interviews each month, and 95% of its interviews took place in November and December 2025, when the separate sample of 22 to 26 year olds was also interviewed.

title: The data
text:
Good to know before comparing
The four surveys share most of their questions, but they were not designed as one sample. A few differences between them therefore matter whenever answers are compared across surveys, and the explorer lets you check whether a pattern holds in each survey separately.
The age ranges of the two providers overlap only at ages 16 to 18. A difference between Gallup and Survation can thus reflect age as much as the provider, and even at the shared ages the respondents were recruited in different ways.
The variable wave counts the waves within each provider and does not order the surveys in time. Survation W1 was in the field in the summer of 2025, while Gallup W2 was still running, so the fieldwork dates are a better guide to when people answered.
The data are not weighted, and all respondents come from online panels rather than from random samples of the population. The results describe the young people who took part and should not be read as estimates for all young people in the UK.
Each survey also applied its own checks to remove careless or automated answers. Gallup W1, for example, kept respondents who failed its attention check, whereas Survation removed those who failed two checks, so some differences between the surveys may partly come from these rules.
On the scales from 0 to 10, Survation W1 respondents give higher answers than respondents in the other surveys. Averaged over the five party ratings and the left-right scale, for example, they score 5.4, against 4.3 to 4.5 in the other surveys. However, the Survation W1 respondents who took part again a year later already answered much like the other surveys in the first wave, with an average of 4.3. This suggests that the difference reflects who took part in Survation W1 rather than a real difference in attitudes. The insight on left and right shows what this means for one of these scales.
Only 55 Gallup and 72 Survation respondents took part in both waves of their provider, and some of these links are doubtful. In Survation the link runs through the parent’s panel account, and only 39 of the 72 linked respondents are one or two years older in the second wave and report the same gender, so it cannot be ruled out that a sibling answered in some cases. By the same measure, 48 of the 55 Gallup links are plausible.
Finally, the wording of a few questions differs slightly between the surveys. Gallup W1, for instance, introduced the party ratings as parties “in the Parliament of the United Kingdom”, and the other surveys as parties “in the House of Commons”. The codebook notes each of these differences at the question concerned.

title: How young people in the UK think about politics
text:
Interdisciplinary Perspectives on the Politics of Adolescence and Democracy




Between 2024 and 2026, we surveyed young people across the United Kingdom about politics, from 12-year-olds who took part with a parent’s consent to young adults in their mid twenties. On this site, we describe who took part and what they were asked, and you can look at their answers yourself.

title: How young people in the UK think about politics
text:
Four surveys, 2024 to 2026
Two fieldwork providers carried out the surveys for us. Gallup International interviewed 16 to 26 year olds who are members of its online panels, while Survation reached 12 to 18 year olds through their parents, who first gave consent and then handed over to their child. Each provider ran two waves about a year apart. For the second wave, they first invited the respondents of the first wave to take part again and then completed the sample with new respondents, which is why some young people answered our questions twice.











The data How the four surveys were designed, who answered them, and what to keep in mind when comparing them.

Insights Short articles in which we look at selected questions in more detail.

title: Interest, democracy and trust
text: How young people relate to democracy matters for research on political development, because attitudes formed in these years can last. All four surveys asked about political interest and satisfaction with democracy, and three of them asked about trust in five institutions. Because the surveys cover different ages, we compare age groups mostly within a survey.

title: Interest, democracy and trust
text:
Interest in politics

Each line shows one survey. The dots give the share of respondents at each year of age who are fairly or very interested in politics. Ages with fewer than 20 respondents in a survey are left out.










In Gallup W2, the only survey that covers ages 16 to 26, the share who are fairly or very interested in politics rises from 38% at age 16 to 75% at age 26. Gallup W1 shows a similar rise between 16 and 21. Within the Survation surveys, by contrast, interest differs less between 12 and 17 year olds. The two Survation surveys also differ from each other, as 57% of respondents in W1 but only 43% in W2 are fairly or very interested. Interestingly, the 72 Survation W1 respondents who took part again a year later were less interested in W1 (39%) than the other W1 respondents (59%). As with the higher answers of Survation W1 on 0 to 10 scales, this suggests that the difference between the waves partly reflects who took part. Taking all ages of a survey together, young men say slightly more often than young women that they are interested in politics, by 4 to 6 percentage points.

title: Interest, democracy and trust
text:
Satisfaction with democracy

Each bar shows the answers of young women or young men in one survey to the statement “I am satisfied with the way that democracy works in the United Kingdom”, on a scale from 1 (fully disagree) to 7 (fully agree).










In both Gallup surveys, more young people are dissatisfied with the way democracy works in the UK than satisfied (48% against 30% in W1, and 45% against 33% in W2). Among the adolescents in Survation, satisfaction is more common. In Survation W1, more respondents are satisfied than dissatisfied, while in Survation W2 the two groups are of similar size and 35% choose the middle of the scale. In every survey, young women are satisfied less often than young men, for instance 29% against 38% in Gallup W2. Within Gallup W2, satisfaction is also more common among 22 to 26 year olds (40%) than among 18 to 21 year olds (27%). Satisfaction also goes together with interest. Across the surveys, 56% of those who are very interested in politics are satisfied with democracy, compared with 13% of those who are not at all interested.

title: Interest, democracy and trust
text:
Trust in institutions

Each row is one institution, and the dots give its average trust rating in each survey on a scale from 0 (no trust at all) to 10 (complete trust). Survation W2 did not ask these questions.










In all three surveys that asked about trust, the courts and the police are trusted most, while political parties and the media are trusted least. In Gallup W1, for example, trust averages 4.9 for the police but 3.7 for political parties. Survation W1 shows higher trust in every institution, which again fits its higher answers on all 0 to 10 scales. The two Gallup surveys invite a comparison over time, since Gallup W1 was fielded under a Conservative government and Gallup W2 under a Labour government. However, among 18 to 21 year olds, the one age group that both surveys cover well, trust in the UK government is almost the same (3.7 and 3.9). The higher average of Gallup W2 thus comes mainly from its 22 to 26 year olds, who trust the government more (5.0). In both Gallup surveys, young men also trust the government somewhat more than young women, with averages of 4.7 and 4.2 in Gallup W2.

title: Interest, democracy and trust
text:
Ways of governing

Each row is one way of governing a country. The dots give the share of respondents in each survey who find it fairly or very good (5 to 7 on a scale from 1, very bad, to 7, very good).










Large majorities in all surveys find democratic ways of governing good, and elections where every vote counts equally receive the most support, from 69% in Gallup W1 to 90% in Survation W1. At the same time, a strong leader who does not accept interference from anyone is rated good by 40% in Gallup W1, 48% in Gallup W2 and close to three fifths in both Survation surveys. These views are not mutually exclusive. In Survation W2, for example, 52% of respondents rate both equal elections and a strong leader as good. This could mean that some young people read “strong leader” as effective leadership rather than as a rejection of democratic checks, a possibility that these data cannot settle.

title: Interest, democracy and trust
text:
About these data
The four surveys differ in age range, recruitment and timing, and the data are not weighted. Survation W1 respondents give higher answers on 0 to 10 scales, which affects the trust items, and Survation W2 did not ask about trust. The data page explains the design.

title: Left, right and the centre
text: Left and right remain the most common shorthand for describing political positions, even though it is not obvious that young people, and especially adolescents, think about politics in these terms. In all four surveys, we asked respondents to place themselves on a scale from 0 (left) to 10 (right). In this article, we look at how they answered and at whether their answers differ with age and between young women and young men.

title: Left, right and the centre
section: Most answers are close to the centre
text:
Most answers are close to the centre

Each panel shows one survey. The bars give the share of respondents who chose each point of the scale.










Across the four surveys, 49% of respondents placed themselves somewhere between 4 and 6, and the exact middle of the scale was by far the most common answer. This was particularly true of the youngest respondents, 38% of whom chose the midpoint among those aged 12 to 15, compared with 29% among those aged 18 and over. For some, choosing the middle will reflect a genuinely moderate position. For others, it may rather indicate that they do not (yet) think about politics in terms of left and right, which is one reason why averages on this scale should be read with some care.
The average positions in Gallup W1 (4.4), Gallup W2 (5.0) and Survation W2 (5.0) lie close to each other, whereas Survation W1 stands out with an average of 6.1. We do not think that this reflects a real shift to the right among younger adolescents. Respondents in Survation W1 gave higher answers on all scales running from 0 to 10, not only on this one, and those among them who took part again a year later placed themselves much like respondents in the other surveys. The difference thus seems to come from who took part in that survey rather than from what young people of that age think (see The data).

title: Left, right and the centre
text:
Age

Each dot is the average position at one year of age in one survey, with a line for its 95% confidence interval. Ages with fewer than 20 respondents in a survey are left out.










Within Gallup W1 and the two Survation surveys, the average position hardly changes with age. The clearest age pattern appears in Gallup W2, the only survey that covers the full range from 16 to 26. There, the average rises from 4.0 among 16 and 17 year olds to 4.5 among 18 to 21 year olds and 5.5 among those aged 22 to 26. Whether this reflects young people moving to the right as they grow older or differences between generations, a single survey cannot tell. Since the surveys cover different age ranges, a curve drawn across all ages from 12 to 26 would also mix differences between ages with differences between surveys.

title: Left, right and the centre
text:
Gender

Each row compares the average position of young women and young men in one age group of one survey. A longer line means a larger gap. Groups with fewer than 20 respondents are left out.










The gender difference is the most consistent pattern in these data. In every survey and in every age group, young women place themselves further to the left than young men. At the same time, the size of the gap changes with age. Pooled over the surveys, it amounts to only 0.2 points among 12 to 15 year olds, but grows to 0.6 points among 16 and 17 year olds and 0.8 points among 18 to 21 year olds, before narrowing slightly to 0.5 points among those aged 22 to 26. The ideological gap between young women and young men thus seems to open up during the late teens, a period that research on political socialisation regards as formative for political attitudes.

title: Left, right and the centre
section: Left and right, progressive and conservative
text:
Left and right, progressive and conservative
Three of the four surveys also asked respondents where they place themselves between socially progressive (0) and socially conservative (10). Answers on the two scales are related, with a correlation of 0.48, so that young people who see themselves on the left also tend to describe themselves as progressive. However, the relationship is far from perfect, which suggests that, for many young people, social values and a position on the left-right scale do not fully coincide. You can compare both scales by age, gender and survey in the explorer.

title: Left, right and the centre
text:
About these data
The four surveys differ in the ages they cover, in how respondents were recruited and in when they took place, and the data are not weighted. Survation respondents were between 12 and 18 years old and took part through a parent, whereas Gallup respondents were between 16 and 26 and members of an online panel. Differences between the surveys can therefore reflect who took part as much as real differences between groups of young people, which is why we mostly compare groups within the same survey. We describe the design of the surveys in more detail on The data page.

title: Feelings towards the parties
text: Most of the young people in these surveys are too young to vote, so their feelings towards the parties are one of the few ways to see how they relate to party politics. In all four surveys, we asked them to rate five parties on a scale from 0 (strongly dislike) to 10 (strongly like). The surveys took place at different points in the political cycle. Gallup W1 was fielded in May and June 2024, during the general election campaign and under a Conservative government, while all later surveys took place after Labour had come to power (see Who took part).

title: Feelings towards the parties
text:
Which parties young people like

Each panel shows one survey. Bars to the right give the share of respondents who rate a party 7 or higher, bars to the left the share who rate it 3 or lower. Ratings of 4 to 6 are not shown.










Labour is the party that the largest share of respondents like in Gallup W1 (33%) and in both Survation surveys. Gallup W2 is the exception, as 33% of its respondents like the Greens and 29% like Labour. At the other end, the Conservatives and Reform UK are disliked most often. In Gallup W1, 53% rate the Conservatives 3 or lower. In both second waves, Reform UK receives the lowest possible rating of 0 more often than any other party (28% in Gallup W2, 28% in Survation W2). At the same time, 25% of Survation W2 respondents like Reform UK, about as many as like the Greens. This suggests that Reform UK divides young people more sharply than the other parties do.
Survation W1 looks different from the other surveys. Its respondents like every party more often and dislike every party less often, and their average rating across all five parties is 5.2, against 4.2 to 4.4 in the other surveys. This fits the general tendency of Survation W1 respondents to give higher answers on 0 to 10 scales, so it is safer to compare the order of the parties within that survey than their levels across surveys.

title: Feelings towards the parties
text:
Age

Each panel shows one party. The dots give the average rating in each age group of a survey. Groups with fewer than 50 respondents are left out.










Because each survey covers a different age range, age differences are best read within a survey. In Gallup W2, 22 to 26 year olds rate the Conservatives at 4.5 on average, compared with 3.5 among 18 to 21 year olds, and Reform UK at 4.6 compared with 3.3. Labour, too, is rated higher by the older group, while ratings of the Greens hardly differ by age. Since the older group rates almost every party more warmly, this could partly reflect a general tendency to give higher ratings rather than a preference for particular parties. Within the Survation surveys, the age pattern runs the other way, as 16 and 17 year olds rate all five parties slightly lower than 12 to 15 year olds.

title: Feelings towards the parties
text:
Gender

Each row compares the average rating of a party among young women and young men in one survey. A longer line means a larger gap.










The gender differences concern specific parties. In all four surveys, young men rate the Conservatives higher than young women, by 0.2 to 0.8 points, and Reform UK by 0.1 to 0.8 points. In turn, young women in the two Gallup surveys rate the Greens higher than young men, by 0.3 points in W1 and 0.6 points in W2. For Labour and the Liberal Democrats, the gaps are smaller and less consistent. In Survation W1, young men rate every party somewhat higher than young women.

title: Feelings towards the parties
section: The same ages in two waves
text:
The same ages in two waves

Both panels compare Gallup respondents aged 18 to 21 in W1 (spring 2024, light blue) and W2 (mostly late 2025, dark blue). A longer line means a larger difference between the two surveys.










The two Gallup surveys allow a fairer comparison over time, because both include over 800 respondents aged 18 to 21 (821 and 878) recruited in the same way. In this age group, the share who like Labour is 33% in W1 and 22% in W2, while the share who like the Greens rises from 23% to 33%. Interestingly, the share who like Reform UK hardly changes, but the share who give it a rating of 0 rises from 17% to 34%. The two surveys lie on either side of the change from a Conservative to a Labour government. However, the two samples consist of different young people, and the data cannot tell whether the differences reflect the political events of that period or who happened to take part.

title: Feelings towards the parties
text:
About these data
The four surveys differ in age range, recruitment and timing, and the data are not weighted. Gallup W1 introduced the parties as those “in the Parliament of the United Kingdom” and the other surveys as those “in the House of Commons”. The data page explains the design.
